narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 66.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt—roughly a two-in-three risk. That estimate is what drove the rejection, not a judgment about your character or potential.

The strongest factor was your LSAT score. At 38, it was slightly above the average of accepted students, about 37, so this factor actually pushed your prediction toward passing. It was not enough to offset the academic concerns. The next most influential factor was your third-year class-standing decile. At 2, it was far below the accepted-student average of about 5.8, and it pushed strongly toward likely bar failure. Your first-year class-standing decile was the third most important factor. At 2, compared with an accepted-student average of about 6, it also pushed toward failure. Together, the two low class-standing indicators outweighed the modest positive signal from your LSAT.

To move forward, ask admissions for specific feedback, then strengthen the areas the model flagged. Consider additional coursework or a graduate-level program that demonstrates sustained academic performance, especially in rigorous legal or analytical subjects. You might also retake the LSAT to build a clearer margin above the average, and apply to programs that review applications holistically. Address any context behind your early class standing, and reapply only after showing improvement.
